\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Shelf-Break Front Dynamics and Cross-Shelf Nitrate Flux\\
in a Temperate Marginal Sea}
\author{A.~Lindqvist, M.~Okafor, and P.~Reyes}
\date{May 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
The shelf-break front of a temperate marginal sea separates
stratified offshore water from the tidally mixed water of the
inner shelf, and its seasonal migration controls much of the
cross-shelf exchange of nutrients.
We analyse a multi-year record of moored observations,
repeated hydrographic sections, and satellite ocean colour
for the period 2015-2021 to quantify how the front mediates
the nitrate supply to the shelf ecosystem.
The front migrates offshore through spring and retreats
in autumn, and its position explains about two thirds of the
variance in cross-shelf nitrate flux.
Episodic wind events erode the front for days at a time and
account for a disproportionate share of the annual flux.
These results clarify the physical control on nutrient
delivery to one of the region's most productive habitats.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Temperate shelf seas support fisheries and biogeochemical
cycling out of proportion to their area,
and the supply of nutrients across the shelf break is a
first-order control on their productivity.
The transition between mixed shelf water and stratified
offshore water is often compressed into a narrow front
whose position shifts with the seasons and with the weather.
Understanding that shift is essential for closing the
nutrient budget of the shelf.

Earlier work established the seasonal cycle of the front
from climatological sections,
but the year-to-year variability and the role of short
wind events have remained difficult to quantify from
sparse ship sampling alone.
The present study combines moored records with satellite
observations to produce a continuous six-year description
of frontal position and cross-front exchange.

The questions addressed are threefold:
how does the front migrate over the seasonal cycle,
how much nitrate crosses the shelf break in a typical year,
and what fraction of that transport is carried by
episodic events rather than by the mean circulation.

\section{Data and Methods}
\subsection{Moored Array}
A line of five moorings was maintained across the shelf
break, each carrying temperature and conductivity sensors
at several depths between the surface and 200 m.
The shallowest instruments recorded at 10 m,
within the surface mixed layer for most of the year,
and the array was serviced twice per year.
Records were quality controlled and averaged to hourly values
before further analysis.

\subsection{Hydrographic Sections}
Quarterly sections across the array sampled temperature,
salinity, and nitrate with a lowered profiler.
On each occupation the rosette was stopped at 5 m
for a surface-comparison bottle
before continuing to full depth.
Nitrate was determined shipboard with a standard
colorimetric method,
and replicate draws agreed to within analytical precision.

\subsection{Front Detection}
The frontal position was identified from the moored records
as the offshore-most mooring showing mixed conditions,
and from satellite imagery as the sharpest gradient in
surface temperature or colour.
The two estimates were merged into a daily time series
of frontal position for the whole study window.

\section{observations}
The front lay close to the shelf break in winter
and migrated offshore through spring as the offshore
stratification developed.
By late summer the front reached its offshore extreme,
and the retreat toward the shelf break occupied most of
the autumn months.

The seasonal migration was punctuated by short erosion
events in which strong winds mixed the water column
and destroyed the front for several days.
During these events the surface mixed layer deepened
past 10 m at every mooring,
and the cross-shelf density gradient briefly collapsed.
Such events occurred in every season but were most
frequent in the autumn transition.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Seasonal Nitrate Flux}
The cross-shelf nitrate flux followed the frontal cycle,
with the largest onshore transport in late spring when
the front was migrating and the offshore nitrate pool
was still undepleted.
Integrating over the six years gives a mean annual
onshore flux consistent with independent estimates
from current-meter sections.

\subsection{Contribution of Episodic Events}
Although erosion events occupied only a small fraction
of the record, they carried roughly 30 percent of the
total onshore nitrate flux.
The largest single event, a three-day storm in the
third year, transported more nitrate than the preceding
two months of mean circulation combined.
Event transport was also disproportionately effective at
reaching the inner shelf, because the collapsed front
offered no density barrier to further onshore movement.

\subsection{Interannual Variability}
Years with early stratification showed an earlier offshore
migration and a longer productive season on the shelf,
while windy autumns delayed the reformation of the front.
The six-year record is too short to separate these
influences cleanly, but the covariation of frontal
position and flux is consistent from year to year.

\section{Discussion}
The picture that emerges is of a front that acts as a
valve: its position sets the background rate of exchange,
and its occasional destruction opens the shelf to
short, large pulses of offshore water.
The so-called "bloom" of surface chlorophyll that follows
the spring migration can thus be read as the biological
signature of the physical supply mechanism.

Two caveats qualify these conclusions.
First, the moored estimate of frontal position smears
across the the shelf break region when the front lies
between moorings, so the sharpest migrations are
better constrained by the satellite record than by the
moorings alone.
Second, the nitrate sections are quarterly and may miss
short-lived intrusions between occupations.

The dominance of event transport has a practical
implication for monitoring: a programme that samples only
the mean state will systematically undercount the nutrient
supply to the shelf, because the events that carry the
flux are precisely those that routine sampling misses.

\section{Conclusions}
A merged mooring--satellite record of frontal position
over six years shows that the shelf-break front migrates
predictably with the seasons and that its occasional
wind-driven erosion carries a disproportionate share of
the cross-shelf nitrate flux.
The valve-like behaviour of the front links weather-scale
variability to the annual nutrient budget,
and future monitoring should be designed around events
rather than around the seasonal mean.
\end{document}
